# Report: Bertone & Hooper, "A History of Dark Matter"

**The question, frozen.** The title and opening put one question central: *how did dark matter become accepted as part of the standard cosmological model?* Not "is dark matter real," and not "who said the phrase first" — the paper says that second one is not the question. Range: late 19th century to 2016, focus on the 20th. Asked: what produced the acceptance. Note the file is cut off mid-Chapter V; Chapters VI–IX and the conclusions are not in front of me, so I mark only what was supplied.

**The explanation, in the authors' words.**
P1 — Independent dynamical discrepancies at many scales: local star kinematics, clusters, rotation curves.
P2 — The famous account is wrong: Zwicky's and Rubin's work was "in continuity with the contemporary scientific literature."
P3 — Rivals ruled out by measurement: gas (X-ray), MACHOs (microlensing), baryons (light-element abundances), MOND (successes and failures).
P4 — Convergence of particle physics and cosmology, cosmology becoming a science, and simulations "led most of the scientific community to accept the idea that dark matter was made of non-baryonic particles."
P5 — "Dark matter" shifted from adjective to proper noun, "reflecting... a sociological change in the underlying scientific culture."
P6 — "A continuously changing landscape," in which scientists were "repeatedly forced to revise their theories and beliefs."

## Part by part

| Part | Mark | What holds it, or what could replace it |
|---|---|---|
| P1 multi-scale dynamical discrepancy | **Held** (by the job "why a mass discrepancy at all") | Swap Coma for Virgo, M31 for M33: the story still runs. So the named system is loose; what is held is the more general thing — *a virial or rotation estimate giving more mass than the light does*. Rename the part to that. |
| P2 the pioneer anecdote is incomplete | **Held** | By a dated source: Zwicky uses "dark matter" in an earlier 1933 cosmic-ray paper. Testable, and tested. |
| P3 rivals excluded | **Borrowed** | Each exclusion rests on another explanation not tested here. The baryonic exclusion rests on Big Bang nucleosynthesis; microlensing rests on the microlensing explanation. Name them. |
| P4 convergence → non-baryonic particles | **Held if** | Held only by the job "why particles, not faint stars." That job is itself in doubt, because its main prop (P3's BBN leg) is borrowed. What would settle it: the abundance numbers supplied and checked. |
| P5 word-shift | **Held** | Traced through dated primary sources, and it pays off — it stops modern meaning being read back into Zwicky. |
| P5 culture-shift half | **Loose** | "Sociological change in the scientific culture" could be swapped for "funding priorities" or "new instruments" with nothing in the text changing. No gauge named. |
| P6 "repeatedly forced to revise" | **Loose** | Flip it: the same sentence covers a history in which MOND won. See below. |

## Whole-explanation checks

**Change list.** What it covers: new instruments and measurements (telescope, photography, 21-cm radio, X-ray, microlensing, Hipparcos/Gaia); and the rival outcomes that could have mattered — Coma at 80 km/s instead of 1000, the 1961 Santa Barbara split over instability, Oort's local verdict ("no dark matter, or not so much as shining matter"), gas limited to under 2%, BBN excluding baryons, MOND's failures. This is a real list: it could have gone the other way, and the paper says where. Left out openly: the authors state they are "not professional historians" and fall short of the profession's standards — a stated limit, fine. Left out in silence: nothing I can see in the supplied chapters.

**Flip.** Ask whether the account would have fitted the opposite. P6 plainly would — it is a catch-all ("a continuously changing landscape"). It is allowed only with a gauge, and the gauges exist for Chapters III–IV (each revision tied to a named measurement) but thin out later. P1–P3 could not have fitted the opposite: had Coma come out at 80 km/s and the abundances allowed baryons, there would be no accepted non-baryonic dark matter. The flip separates the held parts from the loose frame.

**Direction.** A backwards-history risk: telling the story from today's acceptance. The paper partly guards against this — it denies "not commonly accepted, nor disregarded," lets Rubin credit Roberts, and records that her optical curves left the halo question open (Kalnajs, Kent). But the preface's "led to the establishment... among the pillars" runs from the result back to the causes.

**Answer hidden in the starting points.** "Dark matter" is named as a proper noun up front, then "explained." That is legitimate — it is the endpoint of the question asked. But "the emergence of cosmology as a science" is a label until cashed; it is only partly cashed (the 1983 Fermilab group, the P5 "Cosmic Frontier").

**Jobs and ownership.** The authors chose the jobs (acceptance of *non-baryonic particle* dark matter) and built parts to fit. They mark their own jobs honestly, which helps.

**Pairs that pull.** (i) "A few pioneers" against "in continuity" — the paper gives way to continuity, and says so. (ii) Local estimates saying little dark matter against clusters demanding a great deal — a real pull, resolved by halo geometry (small local density, extended halo). (iii) Who-published-first disputes against the data-driven thesis — gives way to data.

**Look inside.** For a history, the workings are the reasons people gave at the time. The paper uses scanned primary sources and interviews, so it partly reaches inside. But "the reader does not have to ask themselves whether the authors might have in mind white dwarfs" is a claim about today's readers, asserted, not tested.

**Rivals.** Baryonic matter and MOND are both built and both struck down with named observations. Good practice.

**Where the parts came from.** *Fitted:* the Zwicky-and-Rubin anecdote, fitted to popularity; the paper cuts it. *Built:* the primary-source timeline, and the word-shift, both worked out with the sources in view and able to be caught out. *Asserted:* the culture-shift and "repeatedly forced to revise." *Borrowed:* BBN and the structure-formation simulations.

## What would make it harder to vary

1. Give P6 a gauge: for each decade, name one measurement that would have kept the baryonic or MOND option alive, and show the text naming it. A sentence that can fail is worth more than a sentence that fits everything.
2. Mark the BBN leg as borrowed, or supply the abundances that exclude baryons. Two of the strongest parts lean on it.

## What this does not show

Hard to vary is not true. A history can be tightly argued and still misread what scientists thought — and much of this paper's holding power is borrowed from the very papers it narrates. Passing here certifies nothing about the past.

## One next step

Take Chapter IV and, for each decade, write the change that would have saved dark matter's rivals. Where a decade has no such change, that decade is being told backwards from the result.
